1.0.0.en: Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ: he did not call himself an apostle but a prisoner. Why?

1.0.1.en: 1- Because he was imprisoned in Rome at that time.

1.0.2.en: 2- He speaks humbly with Philemon and begs him to forgive Onesimus, not with the authority of an apostle but with the humility of a loving friend.

1.0.3.en: 3- By his own imprisonment he shares with Onesimus the slave in his bondage, and so shows his love for him.

1.0.4.en: 4- Imprisonment is a fellowship of love with Christ, who redeemed us and bore our sins for us, so that he may call Philemon to bear with Onesimus's wrong and to forgive him.

1.0.5.en: Timothy our brother: out of Paul's humility, he makes his disciple Timothy a partner with him in sending the Epistle to Philemon, and to show him that the Church, in the persons of Paul and Timothy, asks Philemon to forgive Onesimus.

1.0.6.en: Philemon our dearly beloved and fellowlabourer: Philemon means loving. Paul describes him as beloved to Paul's heart, and in humility he does not call him his disciple but describes him as a fellow worker with him in the ministry.

1.1.0.en: To our beloved Apphia: she is Philemon's wife, and, as a member of the Church, Paul calls her beloved with his fatherhood to her, to God and to the Church.

1.1.1.en: Archippus our fellowsoldier: Archippus is the son of Philemon, and he was a servant in the Church of Colossae as a soldier of Jesus Christ, as Paul spoke to him about his ministry in (Col 4:17); he may have been a priest.

1.1.2.en: The church in thy house: Philemon was rich and his house was spacious, so he received the believers in his house to pray their liturgies and hold their special gatherings, since churches were held in houses before independent churches were built.

1.2.0.en: He sends them the grace of God and His peace to fill their hearts.

1.2.1.en: If you want to win others, express your love for them in gentle words and speak with them humbly, and they will be drawn to your words.

1.3.s.en: (2) His love for Philemon and his praise of him

1.3.0.en: St. Paul begins, as is his custom in all his epistles, by encouraging Philemon with thanksgiving to God for his virtues, and likewise he shows his love for him by constantly remembering him in his prayers, since chains do not hinder him from loving his son Philemon. By beginning with this love he makes Philemon ashamed and moves him to love Onesimus and forgive him when he asks this of him a few verses later.

1.4.0.en: Paul's love also appears in that the chains did not keep him from hearing the news of Philemon, which he heard from Onesimus or from other believers who came to him in Rome from Colossae, and what he heard includes two things:

1.4.1.en: 1- His love toward all the saints, that is, the believers sanctified in Christ, for he received them as a church in his house.

1.4.2.en: 2- His faith in Christ, which he expressed in love toward the believers. Love is mentioned before faith because it is the form visible to people, and so it declares that within Philemon is a strong faith in Christ, who gave His life as a ransom for him; and this faith moved Philemon to offer love to the whole Church.

1.5.0.en: Philemon's faith is not theoretical but active, working by love toward the believers, and this helps God to reveal to him new depths of goodness and righteousness in his life, so that he is driven to more good works for the sake of Christ.

1.6.0.en: Paul shows his joy, which comforts him amid the afflictions of his prison, and the cause of this joy is the deep feelings of love from the believers toward Philemon, who cares for them and receives them in his house; and he humbly calls him a brother and not a son.

1.6.1.en: Open your heart with love toward everyone, to show them Christ in practice. Encourage those who are far away and those who have no one to care for them, and so you will be an image of Christ, who went about doing good in every place.

1.7.s.en: (3) His request that Onesimus be received

1.7.0.en: Wherefore: because of your love for the believers in Colossae and your receiving the Church in your house. Though I might be much bold in Christ to enjoin thee: that is, he is able, by his authority as an apostle of Christ, to command his son Philemon.

1.7.1.en: That which is convenient: what is fitting for Philemon and good for the Church.

1.8.0.en: Paul did not use his authority as an apostle or as a bishop responsible for the Church, but approaches Philemon with love to beseech him gently, and he stirs Philemon's feelings of love toward him by describing himself as aged, for he was then nearly sixty years old, so he is older than Philemon, and it is customary to respect elders and value their words, especially if they are spiritual fathers marked by love. He also moves his feelings by making clear that he is a prisoner for Christ's sake. So he asks his disciple Philemon and says to him: for the sake of the love of Christ, and as one advanced in age like a father to you, and now bound in prison, I beg you to forgive Onesimus.

1.9.0.en: He asks Philemon to forgive Onesimus and describes the latter as his son, whom he begat in his bonds, that is, who believed at his hands during his first imprisonment in Rome. He is not an ordinary son, but a son of old age and a son of chains, so he is dear to his heart.

1.9.1.en: Perhaps Philemon was astonished on reading these words, because a slave was then considered like an animal, whereas Paul speaks of him as a son close to his heart. This of course had a great effect on Philemon, because by his sonship to Paul Onesimus became a brother of Philemon and not a slave, for their father is one, namely Paul. More than this, Onesimus is a new son of Paul and a younger brother of Philemon, who deserves his kindness and compassion.

1.10.0.en: The word Onesimus in Greek means profitable, but he had previously behaved badly during his slavery under Philemon, and stole from him and fled, so his conduct changed his name, that is, to unprofitable. But after he believed at the hands of Paul, he became his servant in Rome, and Paul sent him to Philemon, announcing his new character, that it is like his name, that is, that he will be profitable to Philemon as a beloved brother who serves him faithfully, and this of course with the agreement of Onesimus himself.

1.11.0.en: As Paul sends Onesimus back to Philemon after his life and conduct were changed by faith, he declares that he is offering his son, who is a part of him, and who carries for him deep feelings of love and has been bound to him as an assisting servant; that is, he returns to Philemon a new person, very dear to Paul's heart, and asks him to receive him with his love.

1.11.1.en: Try to show the virtues of others, so that you may soften the angry, when they see good qualities in those who have erred and so receive them. But do not forget first to sympathize with the angry and to praise them, so that they accept your words and your good view of those who have erred; and thus by love you bring hearts together.

1.12.0.en: The bonds of the gospel: the imprisonment that Paul endures for the sake of preaching the Gospel of Christ.

1.12.1.en: In order that Paul might declare to Philemon the change that took place in Onesimus, he made clear that he trusts Onesimus and his faithfulness in serving him during his imprisonment in Rome, and this trust is no less than his trust in Philemon himself and his service, so much so that he substituted the service of Onesimus for the service of Philemon to him. So here he declares the equality of the two, Philemon and Onesimus, before God as His servants. He also shows Philemon's responsibility, out of his love for Paul, to serve him in his prison, but Onesimus completed this service in place of Philemon, to show the worth and greatness of Onesimus as a servant, and that he fills the lack caused by Philemon's not being beside Paul to serve him. Likewise Paul's care in respecting Philemon's authority as master over his slave Onesimus appears, for all the foregoing trust on Paul's part was merely a wish, and he would carry it out only with Philemon's permission, and therefore he sent his slave Onesimus back to him. All this is to raise the worth of Onesimus before Philemon, so that he forgives him his wrong in stealing and fleeing from him and treats him as a spiritual brother.

1.13.0.en: Without thy mind: your forgiveness of Onesimus and your agreement that he serve me.

1.13.1.en: Thy benefit: your giving your slave Onesimus to serve me.

1.13.2.en: As it were of necessity: Onesimus's staying with Paul, which would embarrass Philemon, and using his slave Onesimus in Paul's service without asking his permission.

1.13.3.en: Paul shows the importance of respecting the freedom of the other in sending Onesimus to Philemon, so that if Philemon forgave him and of his own will sent him back to Paul to serve him, it would be by his choice and not by compulsion.

1.14.0.en: Paul explains the wisdom of God in allowing the sin of Onesimus, which was stealing and fleeing, and he expresses it in a gentle way, saying he departed, and he expresses the period during which he fled, which is short compared with eternity, as for a season (an hour), so that Onesimus might repent and believe in Christ and enjoy blessed eternity with Philemon. Thus Onesimus is not parted from Philemon, not only for the whole of life, but they will be together in the Kingdom forever.

1.15.0.en: By the faith of Onesimus and the change of his life, he became a spiritual servant and a member of the body of Christ, so he became a brother of Paul, who is a father and teacher of Philemon; all the more, then, Onesimus becomes a beloved brother to Philemon, not only in the flesh, that is, while remaining in the service of slavery with Philemon, but as a member of the Church, so that he is a brother to Philemon in God. For Philemon could keep him as a slave, and forgive him and treat him with love as his brother, or free him and give him liberty to leave him and live in any place.

1.16.0.en: Paul appeals to Philemon's sympathy and love and raises the worth of Onesimus, saying to Philemon: since you consider me a partner with you in the faith and in membership of the body of Christ, and this is humility on Paul's part to make Philemon ashamed, since Paul is a father and teacher of Philemon and not merely a partner, in any case he asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as he would receive Paul, with the same rank, respect and esteem.

1.16.1.en: Respecting the feelings of others and humility in speaking with them make it easy for you to win them. So be careful to show your esteem for everyone, to respect his opinion, to listen to him attentively and to carry it out as far as you can.

1.17.0.en: The flight of Onesimus, who was a slave owned by Philemon, was a wrong and a theft from him because he was a slave, in addition to the money that he stole from Philemon to travel with it from Colossae to Rome and to live on it there. This theft is considered a debt on Onesimus, but he does not have the means to pay the debt after he believed and repented, so Paul steps forward with his fatherhood to promise Philemon to repay the debt that is on Onesimus.

1.18.0.en: I Paul have written it with mine own hand: Paul was not accustomed to write with his own hand because of the weakness of his eyesight, but here he took care to write with his own hand as an acknowledgment of the debt, so that this is considered a bond or a cheque on Paul. The Apostle Paul reassures Philemon that he is responsible for repaying the debt that is on Onesimus, but at the same time he reminds Philemon that he believed at his hands, so he is indebted to him for the new life that he lives in Christ, which is more precious than all the wealth of the world; that is, he makes Philemon ashamed, since he is indebted to Paul more than Paul's debt to him through this stolen money.

1.19.0.en: Paul hopes to rejoice in the fruits of the spiritual life that are in Philemon, by his forgiving his thieving, fugitive slave, and this is what gives rest to Paul's heart, that is, Philemon's love and Onesimus's settling into a quiet life without debts or problems.

1.20.0.en: St. Paul urges Philemon to forgive Onesimus by saying to him: I trust in your obedience to me, and indeed he calls him to something more, that is, the release and emancipation of Onesimus, and this is what he actually did, as the history of the Church and the Synaxarium tell us.

1.20.1.en: May the desires of your heart be to do good with every person, and may you not rest except in the rest of all, and may you strive for the salvation of their souls and their attachment to the Church, so that they enjoy a life of assurance with Christ.

1.21.s.en: (4) Preparing the house and the closing greetings

1.21.0.en: But withal: in addition to pardoning Onesimus.

1.21.1.en: Paul expected to be released soon from his prison in Rome, and in his fatherhood he longed to visit the Church of Colossae to look after it and care for it. So he asked Philemon, because of his characteristic of hospitality to the Church and to strangers, and because of his friendship with him, to prepare a place for him in his house to stay in during the time of his presence in Colossae. Paul's humility appears in his relying on the prayers of Philemon, his wife Apphia and his son Archippus, that God may release him from his prison and grant him the grace of visiting the Church of Colossae.

1.22.0.en: He closes the Epistle with greetings from his disciples, the servants known to Philemon, and perhaps by this he also asks their intercession for pardon for Onesimus. He mentions among them Epaphras and describes him as my fellowprisoner, which means either that he was imprisoned with Paul at the same time in Rome, or that he was a servant to Paul during his imprisonment, for he is a prisoner of Christ and of His ministry, and he is the servant and founder of the Church of Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis.

1.23.0.en: Marcus: he is Mark the Apostle, the preacher of Egypt, and the writer of the Gospel called by his name.

1.23.1.en: Aristarchus: from Thessalonica, and one of the disciples of Paul who accompanied him on his missionary journeys, and he was with him in his first imprisonment in Rome.

1.23.2.en: Demas: one of the disciples of Paul who accompanied him on his missionary journeys, but in the second imprisonment of the Apostle Paul in Rome in the year (67 A.D.) he could not bear to continue the toil of ministry, so he left Paul and returned to his former life in the world and went to Thessalonica (2 Tim 4:10). Lucas: he is one of the disciples of Paul and the writer of the Gospel called by his name and of the Book of the Acts of the Apostles.

1.24.0.en: He closes the Epistle with the request that the grace of God be with Philemon and his household, to bind him to God and to make him grow in love for all. This Epistle was carried to Philemon by his slave Onesimus, who became a servant in the Church and afterwards a bishop.

1.24.1.en: Rely on the prayers of the saints and the prayers of those around you, to move God's heart toward you, and He will grant you His many gifts and the desire of your heart, because God rejoices in your love for the saints and for your brothers in the Church, and rejoices also in your humility.
